content: Antibiotics disrupt the natural balance of gut microbiota, often leading to antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD). Probiotics are hypothesized to prevent AAD by strengthening the gut barrier, restoring gut microflora, and through other mechanisms. The primary aim of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of probiotics, regardless of strain or dose, in preventing AAD in children. A comprehensive search of multiple databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, and others, was conducted up to May 28, 2018. Randomized, parallel, controlled trials involving children aged 0 to 18 years who were receiving antibiotics were included. These trials compared probiotics to placebo, alternative prophylaxis, or no treatment, and measured the incidence of AAD. Data from 33 studies involving 6,352 participants were analyzed. Probiotics assessed included various strains such as Bacillus spp., Bifidobacterium spp., Clostridium butyricum, Lactobacilli spp., Lactococcus spp., Leuconostoc cremoris, Saccharomyces spp., and Streptococcus spp., either alone or in combination. The risk of bias was high in 20 studies and low in 13 studies. The results showed that probiotics significantly reduced the incidence of AAD. After 5 days to 12 weeks of follow-up, 8% of children in the probiotic group experienced AAD compared to 19% in the control group (Risk Ratio [RR] 0.45, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 0.36 to 0.56; Number Needed to Treat for Benefit [NNTB] = 9, 95% CI 7 to 13). This evidence was of moderate certainty. Even when accounting for participants lost to follow-up, the benefit of probiotics remained statistically significant. In an intention-to-treat analysis, the incidence of AAD was 12% in the probiotic group compared to 19% in the control group (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.77). Subgroup analysis revealed that high-dose probiotics (≥ 5 billion CFUs per day) were more effective than low-dose probiotics (< 5 billion CFUs per day). In high-dose studies, the incidence of AAD was 8% in the probiotic group compared to 23% in the control group (RR 0.37, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.46). For low-dose studies, the incidence was 8% in the probiotic group compared to 13% in the control group (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.01). The benefit of high-dose probiotics remained significant even when accounting for loss to follow-up. Adverse events were reported in 24 trials involving 4,415 participants. No serious adverse events were attributed to probiotics. Minor adverse events, such as rash, nausea, gas, flatulence, abdominal bloating, and constipation, were reported in 4% of probiotic participants compared to 6% of control participants. The certainty of this evidence was low. Probiotics also reduced the mean duration of diarrhea by nearly one day (Mean Difference [MD] -0.91 days, 95% CI -1.38 to -0.44). However, this evidence was of low certainty. One study examined microbiome characteristics and found no significant differences in changes when probiotics were used alongside antibiotics. In conclusion, probiotics appear to have a moderate protective effect against AAD in children, with an NNTB of 9. High-dose probiotics (≥ 5 billion CFUs per day), such as Lactobacillus rhamnosus or Saccharomyces boulardii, were particularly effective, with an NNTB of 6. However, further large, well-designed, multi-center randomized trials are needed to confirm these findings. The safety profile of probiotics was favorable, with no serious adverse events reported in the included studies. Nonetheless, caution is warranted in severely debilitated or immunocompromised children, as observational studies outside this review have reported serious adverse events in such populations.
